# Meghiya Sutta (Ud 4.1 (PTS Ud 34))

**ID:** Ud 4.1 (PTS Ud 34)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Meghiya Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ud4.1
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0503m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Meghiya Sutta* (Ud 4.1; PTS Ud 34–37) is the opening discourse of the fourth chapter of the Udāna [Shaw 2006]. Set at Cālikā on Cālikā Hill, the narrative depicts Venerable Meghiya serving as the Buddha's attendant [Shaw 2006; Tan 2002, 2004]. Despite the Buddha's admonition to wait for another monk to arrive, Meghiya departs for a mango grove to practice solitary meditation, only to find himself overwhelmed by unwholesome, discursive thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and harm [SuttaCentral; Shaw 2006]. Returning to the Buddha, he receives instruction on the five conditions that bring immature freedom of mind (*cetovimutti*) to maturity: cultivating good spiritual friendship (*kalyāṇamitta*), ethical restraint (*sīla*), talk directed to dispassion and mental clarity, energetic exertion (*vīriya*), and penetrative wisdom into arising and passing away (*paññā*) [Saitanaporn 2009; Thich Thien Chau 1996]. The Buddha further instructs that four specific meditations must be developed: the contemplation of foulness/ugliness (*asubha*) to eliminate lust, loving-kindness (*mettā*) to remove ill-will, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*) to cut off discursive thoughts, and reflection on impermanence (*anicca*) to uproot the conceit "I am" and realize non-self (*anattā*) [Shaw 2006; Conze; Sujato 2012; Melnikova 2014; Pa-Auk Sayadaw]. The discourse concludes with an inspired utterance (*udāna*) [Shaw 2006].

Curated parallels include a nearly verbatim Pali parallel in the *Navakanipāta* of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 9.3) and a Chinese parallel in the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 56) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly corroborates these relationships, identifying massive Pali-internal text reuse with AN 9 (122 matches, covering §1.2–17.1_1 with §3.1.1–3.15.2 at 0.91 similarity) and automatic alignment with the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26, best score 65) [DharmaNexus]. Resembling verse parallels are preserved in the *Cittavarga* chapters of various *Udānavarga* recensions (UV 31, UVS 31, Uv Kg 31, T 212, and T 213) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also traces widespread text reuse across the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 5, AN 8, AN 6), *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 45, SN 46, SN 35), and later commentaries such as the *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā* and *Majjhimanikāye Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

Commentarial tradition explains Meghiya's sudden influx of unskillful thoughts by noting that he had lived as a king in that specific mango grove in a past life, exposing him to latent memories of sensual pleasures and royal cruelties [Shaw 2006]. The narrative is also reused in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [Burlingame 1921]. Modern scholars and commentators frequently treat the sutta as an essential exposition of spiritual friendship, the necessity of matching meditation subjects to temperament, and the sequence of meditative antidotes [Shaw 2006; Tan 2002, 2004; Sujato 2012].
